title: How to Use a Spurtle to Mix Sourdough Garlic Bread Dough
meta_description: Master the art of sourdough garlic bread recipe mixing with a wooden spurtle. Learn step‑by‑step tips for flawless dough and perfect crust.
html:
When you’re tackling a sourdough garlic bread recipe mixing routine, the tool you reach for can make the difference between a shaggy, uneven loaf and a beautifully airy, fragrant loaf. A wooden spurtle – specifically the 2 PCS Wooden Spurtle Spatula for Sourdough Starter, Wood Danish Dough Whisk – is the unsung hero that handles sticky starters, scrapes every last bit of dough from the bowl, and keeps your jars pristine.

Why a Spurtle Beats a Traditional Whisk for Sourdough

A spurtle’s slender, tapered shape lets you stir without incorporating too much air too early. In sourdough, you want to develop gluten gradually; a whisk can over‑beat the dough, tearing the delicate gluten network that gives the bread its chew. The wooden spurtle also stays cool, preventing the dough from warming up while you’re mixing the starter or the final dough.

Preparing Your Starter and Ingredients

Before you even think about the dough, make sure your starter is active. Feed it 4–6 hours before you plan to mix, and look for those bubbles that signal readiness. While the starter is rising, measure out the flour, water, salt, and of course, the garlic‑infused butter that will finish the loaf.

  • 200 g active sourdough starter
  • 500 g bread flour
  • 350 g water (room temperature)
  • 10 g sea salt
  • 4 cloves garlic, minced
  • 50 g softened butter

Having everything measured and ready (the “baker’s mise en place”) saves you from scrambling once the dough comes together.

Mixing the Dough with a Wooden Spurtle

Start by adding the water and starter to a large, non‑reactive bowl. Use the 2 PCS Wooden Spurtle Spatula set – the skinny spurtle for stirring and the Danish‑style dough stick for scraping – to combine them. The spurtle’s flat edge glides through the thick starter, pulling it into the water without splashing.

Once the starter and water are fully incorporated, sprinkle the flour over the mixture. Grab the spurtle and begin a slow, clockwise motion, folding the flour into the liquid. The key is to work in short bursts: 30 seconds of stirring, then pause to let the flour hydrate. After about 5 minutes, the mixture will look shaggy and slightly sticky – that’s the autolyse phase, where gluten begins to form on its own.Now add the salt and minced garlic. Use the narrow tip of the Danish dough stick to push the seasoning into the dough without tearing it. Continue stirring with the spurtle until the dough pulls away from the sides of the bowl, forming a loose ball.

Developing Gluten Without Over‑Mixing

At this stage, you could switch to a stand mixer, but the spurtle lets you stay in control. Transfer the dough onto a lightly floured surface and perform a series of “stretch‑and‑fold” motions every 30 minutes for the next two hours. The spurtle’s smooth wooden surface is gentle on the dough, preventing the crust from forming prematurely.

If the dough sticks to your hands, dip the spurtle in a little water and use it to lift the dough away from the work surface. This technique keeps the dough’s temperature low, which is especially important in a warm kitchen.

Shaping, Butter‑Garlic Topping, and Baking

When the dough has roughly doubled in size, gently deflate it and shape it into a loaf or a round boule. Place the dough on a parchment‑lined baking sheet. Spread the softened garlic butter evenly over the top, then use the spurtle’s flat side to create shallow furrows. Those grooves allow the butter to seep into the crust, creating pockets of flavor.

Slide the bread into a preheated 450°F (230°C) oven. Bake for 20 minutes, then lower the temperature to 400°F (205°C) and continue baking another 15–20 minutes, or until the crust is a deep golden brown and the internal temperature reads 200°F (93°C). While the bread bakes, use the spurtle to scrape any leftover garlic butter from the jar – the non‑scratch wooden tip won’t dull your cookware.

Cleaning and Caring for Your Spurtle

After the bread cools, rinse the spurtle under warm water and wipe it dry with a lint‑free cloth. Because it’s wooden, avoid soaking it for long periods; a quick hand wash preserves the grain and prevents warping. Occasionally rub a tiny amount of food‑grade mineral oil into the wood to maintain its natural sheen and keep it from absorbing odors.

FAQ

Can I use a metal whisk instead of a spurtle?

Yes, but a metal whisk will incorporate more air early on, which can lead to a tougher crumb. The wooden spurtle gives you a gentler stir and better temperature control.

Is the spurtle safe for silicone or non‑stick cookware?

Absolutely. The smooth wood won’t scratch silicone mats, non‑stick pans, or ceramic jars, making it ideal for scraping the last bits of starter or butter.

How often should I oil the wooden spurtle?

Oil it lightly once a month, or whenever the wood looks dry. A few drops of mineral oil rubbed in will keep it resilient and odor‑free.
